text: The management of scientific research in a developing country presents unique challenges. Resources are limited, talent is scarce, and the temptation to spread efforts too thin across too many projects is ever-present. At PRL and ISRO, we have learned that focus is essential. It is better to do a few things exceptionally well than to do many things poorly. This principle of strategic concentration guides our resource allocation decisions. We identify the areas where we can make a genuine contribution to world science, and we invest heavily in those areas. In everything else, we collaborate with international partners rather than duplicating their efforts.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Lecture at National Science Academy, 1970

text: The challenge of poverty in India is not a lack of resources but a failure of organisation and technology deployment. India has abundant natural resources, a large and growing workforce, and a strong tradition of enterprise. What we lack is the systematic application of scientific knowledge and management expertise to our developmental challenges. This is precisely the gap that our institutions — PRL, ISRO, IIM, ATIRA — are designed to fill. Each institution is a node in a network of capability that, taken together, gives India the tools to transform itself from a predominantly agrarian economy into a modern, technologically capable nation.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Address on Poverty and Technology, 1969

text: When I think about the future of India, I see a country transformed by technology but rooted in its ancient values. I see villages connected by satellite communication, where every child has access to quality education, every farmer has access to weather forecasts and market information, and every citizen has access to healthcare guidance. I see cities powered by nuclear energy, managed by world-class institutions, and connected to the global economy through advanced telecommunications. But I also see a country that has not lost its soul — that retains its respect for nature, its commitment to non-violence, its celebration of diversity, and its deep spiritual traditions. This synthesis of the modern and the traditional is India's unique gift to the world.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Vision Statement for India's Future, 1971

text: The training of scientists and engineers is the most critical investment a developing nation can make. Machines can be imported; technology can be licensed; even factories can be built with foreign assistance. But the ability to understand, adapt, improve, and innovate with technology cannot be imported. It must be grown, nurtured, and cultivated through rigorous education and hands-on experience. This is why I spend so much of my time on educational institutions and training programmes. Every young scientist who learns to think independently, every engineer who learns to solve problems creatively, is a permanent addition to India's national capability.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Address at ISRO Training Centre Inauguration, 1970

text: The Sarabhai family has a long tradition of combining business enterprise with social responsibility. My father, Ambalal Sarabhai, was a successful textile industrialist who was deeply influenced by Mahatma Gandhi. He supported the independence movement, encouraged education for women and the disadvantaged, and used his wealth for the public good. My mother, Sarala Devi, was a social reformer who championed education and women's rights. Growing up in this environment instilled in me the conviction that privilege carries responsibility, and that the greatest use of any capability — whether in business, science, or public life — is in service to society.

The concept of the 'scientific temper' is central to India's modernisation. Jawaharlal Nehru spoke eloquently about the need for a scientific approach to life — an approach based on evidence, reason, and critical thinking rather than superstition, dogma, and blind tradition. I share this vision completely. The scientific temper is not about rejecting tradition wholesale. It is about subjecting our beliefs and practices to rational scrutiny, keeping what is valuable and discarding what is harmful. A society with a strong scientific temper is better equipped to solve its problems, resist demagoguery, and make informed decisions about its future.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Essay on Scientific Temper, 1966

text: The planning and execution of large-scale projects requires a discipline that transcends individual brilliance. At ISRO, we have developed a system of project management that ensures every task is defined, every timeline is realistic, every dependency is identified, and every risk is assessed. We use network analysis techniques — PERT and CPM — to manage the complexity of projects involving hundreds of engineers working on dozens of subsystems simultaneously. This systematic approach to project management is one of the most important things we have learned from our international collaborations, and it is now deeply embedded in our organisational culture.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Paper on Project Management at ISRO, 1969

text: I have always believed that the quality of an institution is determined by the quality of the people it attracts. This is why recruitment is so important. At PRL and ISRO, we do not merely advertise positions and wait for applications. We actively seek out the best talent — visiting universities, attending conferences, reading journals, and asking our existing staff for recommendations. When we find a promising young scientist or engineer, we move quickly to recruit them, offering not necessarily the highest salary but the most exciting opportunities. The best people are motivated not by money but by the chance to do meaningful work on challenging problems.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Lecture on Talent Recruitment, 1967
